The usual choice is be- tween treatment with propofol, midazolam, or a short- acting barbiturate anaesthetic such as pentobarbital or thiopental.3-10,22 The anaesthetic should be continued for 12 to 24 hours after the last clinical or electrographic seizure and the dose then gradually reduced.5 Some con- sider that all patients unresponsive to first-line therapy with a benzodiazepine should be considered refractory and proceed to treatment with propofol or midazolam.6 • Other drugs tried in refractory status include the inhala- tional anaesthetics desflurane and isoflurane.23 Tiagab- ine and ketamine have also been suggested,6 as has val- proate,7,22 and there are a few reports of responses to levetiracetam24 and topiramate.25-27 Evidence to support the management of nonconvulsive forms of status epilepticus (NCSE) is scanty. The BNF rec- ommends that usual oral antiepileptics should initially be continued or restarted in patients with incomplete loss of awareness. Otherwise, it has been suggested that manage- ment should be as for convulsive status,6 albeit less aggres- sive,28 with intravenous benzodiazepines the first choice for initial management.4-6,11,28 Subsequent management will probably be influenced by the drugs known to be ef- fective in the given seizure type. The prognosis depends on the aetiology and level of consciousness: comatose pa- tients with refractory NCSE have a poorer prognosis and general anaesthesia may be appropriate.6 Conscious pa- tients generally have a more favourable outcome and ter- mination of status is considered less urgent; general anaes- thetics should thus be used more cautiously.11,28 1.
